title: Connected Components
description: Build an adjacency list, then DFS from every unvisited node — each fresh DFS launch is one new component. O(V + E).

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.say:
"Let me make sure I have this right: I'm given `n` (the number of nodes, labeled 0 to n-1) and `edges`, a list of `[u, v]` pairs representing undirected edges. I return the number of connected components — groups of nodes mutually reachable via edges, where isolated nodes count as components of size 1."

Then a few quick clarifying questions:
• Undirected — confirmed, right? (If directed, this is a different problem — strongly connected components, Tarjan/Kosaraju.)
• Duplicate edges — `[[0,1],[0,1]]` allowed? Harmless but inflates adj.
• Self-loops `[[0,0]]` — possible? Doesn't change component count.
• Edges referencing nonexistent nodes — guaranteed `0 ≤ u, v < n`?
• `n=0` — return 0 (no nodes, no components)?
sections.why: The directed-vs-undirected question is the load-bearing one — the entire algorithm changes (DFS works for undirected components; you'd need Tarjan or Kosaraju for strongly connected components in directed graphs). The 'self-loop counts as one component for that node' detail is worth confirming; my algorithm handles it without special casing because `dfs(u)` marks `u` seen before recursing, so the self-edge is a no-op. The bounds question is the senior-paranoia one — most candidates assume valid input.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious approach before optimizing.
sections.say:
"The brute force is: for each pair of nodes (i, j), check if there's a path between them, then group nodes by reachability. Computing reachability per pair is O(V + E) per query, with V² pairs — total O(V³ + V²·E). Hopeless past V=100 or so.

The fix is to recognize you only need to mark which 'group' each node belongs to, which falls out of a single DFS pass. You don't need to ask 'is i reachable from j?' for every pair; you ask 'has i been visited yet?' for each i in turn, and if not, you launch a DFS that paints every reachable node with the current group color. Each new launch is a new component."
sections.why: Two reasons to name the per-pair reachability brute force. (1) It's literally what 'count connected components' sounds like before you internalize the algorithm — 'check connectivity between every pair'. (2) It motivates the single-pass insight: 'I don't need pairwise reachability; I need component membership, which is one DFS-per-component.' That reframing is what gets you from O(V³) to O(V + E).

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What signal in the problem points to DFS / Union-Find?
sections.say:
"'Count groups of connected things in an undirected graph' is the textbook connected-components problem, and it has two equally valid solutions:

1. **DFS (or BFS) from each unvisited node.** Build an adjacency list from the edges (pushing BOTH directions because undirected), maintain a `seen` array, then for each i in 0..n-1, if `!seen[i]` launch a DFS that marks everything reachable as seen — and bump the counter. Each fresh launch = one new component. O(V + E) total because each edge is touched at most twice and each node at most once.

2. **Union-Find (DSU).** Initialize each node as its own root, then for every edge `[u, v]` do `union(u, v)`. Count distinct roots at the end. O((V + E) · α(V)) ≈ O(V + E).

DFS is simpler when you already have the adjacency list — fewer moving parts. Union-Find wins when edges arrive in a stream (you can update components incrementally without rebuilding) or when you also need to support 'are i and j in the same component?' queries efficiently. For this problem, both work; I'll go with DFS for clarity, but I'd switch to Union-Find if the problem said 'edges are added one at a time, report component count after each.'"
sections.why: Naming both algorithms AND the decision criterion is the senior move. 'I'll use DFS' is fine; 'I'll use DFS because edges are batched and we have an adj list — but Union-Find would be better for streaming additions' shows you see the family of problems, not just this instance. Interviewers love this — it tells them you've solved enough variants to know when each tool fits. The bidirectional-push rule for the adj list is the one implementation detail that catches people; explicitly calling it out prevents the bug where you only push one direction and DFS only walks one way through each edge.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me trace through a couple of cases to make sure my model is right." Three inputs cover the interesting behaviors — two components of different sizes, an all-isolated case (no edges), and a long chain (one component).

examples.note: Two components — {0,1,2} via 0-1-2 chain, and {3,4} as a pair. The standard case.
examples.trace:
build adj: adj[0]=[1], adj[1]=[0,2], adj[2]=[1], adj[3]=[4], adj[4]=[3]
seen=[F,F,F,F,F], count=0
i=0: !seen[0] → count=1, dfs(0): mark 0, recurse to 1 → mark 1, recurse to 2 → mark 2
i=1: seen → skip
i=2: seen → skip
i=3: !seen[3] → count=2, dfs(3): mark 3, recurse to 4 → mark 4
i=4: seen → skip
return 2

examples.note: Degenerate all-isolated — each node is its own component. Confirms the outer loop drives the count even with no DFS recursion.
examples.trace:
build adj: all five empty lists
seen=[F,F,F,F,F], count=0
i=0: !seen[0] → count=1, dfs(0): mark 0, no neighbors
i=1: !seen[1] → count=2, dfs(1): mark 1, no neighbors
i=2: count=3, mark 2
i=3: count=4, mark 3
i=4: count=5, mark 4
return 5

examples.note: Chain — one DFS launch reaches all five nodes via cascading recursion.
examples.trace:
build adj: adj[0]=[1], adj[1]=[0,2], adj[2]=[1,3], adj[3]=[2,4], adj[4]=[3]
seen=[F,F,F,F,F], count=0
i=0: !seen[0] → count=1, dfs(0):
  mark 0, recurse to 1 → mark 1, recurse to 2 (0 already seen, skipped) → mark 2, recurse to 3 → mark 3, recurse to 4 → mark 4
i=1..4: all seen → skip
return 1

sections.why: Tracing surfaces the two bugs this problem keeps creating. (1) The all-isolated case proves that `count++` lives in the outer-loop guard (`if (!seen[i]) { count++; dfs(i); }`), not inside DFS — if you bumped count per DFS call you'd over-count by the size of each component. (2) The chain case proves that pushing both directions in the adj list is necessary — if you only pushed `adj[u].push(v)` and not the reverse, dfs(0) would walk 0→1→2→3→4 fine (because every forward edge is built), but the SAME chain with edges entered as `[[1,0],[2,1],[3,2],[4,3]]` would fail catastrophically — dfs(0) would mark 0, find adj[0]=[], and stop, leaving 4 'isolated' nodes. The bidirectional push immunizes you against edge-listing order.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Before I declare it done, let me think about edges:
• `n=0, edges=[]` → outer loop doesn't execute, count=0. ✓
• `n=1, edges=[]` → one component, count=1. The outer-loop launch handles it.
• No edges at all (any n) → every node is its own component, count=n. The outer loop drives the entire count.
• All nodes in one big chain — one DFS reaches everything, count=1.
• Duplicate edges `[[0,1],[0,1]]` → adj inflates (`adj[0]=[1,1]`) but the `if (!seen[v])` guard prevents re-recursion. Wasted work, correct answer.
• Self-loops `[[0,0]]` → `adj[0]=[0,0]`, dfs(0) marks 0, then tries to recurse on 0 which is already seen → no-op. Correct.
• Edge referencing out-of-range node (e.g. `edges=[[0, 7]]` with `n=5`) — `adj[7]` is `undefined`. Either pre-validate, or trust the input. Worth flagging.
• Very large `n` (10k+) with a chain-shaped component — recursion depth = chain length, JS stack overflows around 10k frames. Iterative DFS with an explicit stack is the fix."
sections.why: The 'count++ goes in the outer guard, not in DFS' rule is the bug most candidates almost write — and the all-isolated edge case is the cheapest sanity check to expose it (if count were per-dfs-call, the answer would still be 5 because there's one call per isolated node, but the chain example would give 5 instead of 1). The recursion-depth concern is the same one from Number of Islands and Clone Graph — same fix (iterative stack). Calling it out across all three lessons shows pattern-level awareness.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O(V + E). Building the adjacency list is O(E) — one constant-time push per edge in each direction. The outer loop runs V iterations. DFS visits each node exactly once (gated by `seen`) and each edge exactly twice (once from each endpoint). The sum is O(V + E).

Space is O(V + E) — the adjacency list dominates at O(E), `seen` is O(V), and recursion depth is up to V on a path graph.

If you wanted to extend to Union-Find — same problem, different shape: initialize parent[i]=i, then for each `[u, v]` do `union(u, v)`. At the end, count distinct values in `parent.map(x => find(x))`. With path compression and union by rank it's O((V + E) · α(V)). Slightly more complex but it generalizes to streaming-edge-additions, where DFS would have to re-run from scratch on every new edge.

The same template — 'launch DFS from each unvisited node, increment a counter per launch' — shows up in Number of Islands (matrix version), Number of Provinces (adjacency-matrix version), and Friend Circles. All connected-components problems wearing different input clothes."
sections.why: The 'each edge traversed twice' argument is the textbook defense — same as Clone Graph for undirected. The Union-Find pivot is the senior move that earns you the bonus 'when would you switch?' question and the answer ('streaming edge additions'). The cross-reference to Islands and Provinces is what proves you see the algorithm as a template, not this one problem's trick — and it primes the interviewer to ask you about those next, where you can blow them out of the water with the matrix or adjacency-matrix variants.

walkthrough.intro: Step through the DFS-based component count. Watch the adjacency list build (both directions per undirected edge), then the outer scan launch a fresh DFS for every unvisited node — each launch bumps count by one.
trace: yield { line: 1, label: `enter countComponents — n=${n}, edges=${JSON.stringify(edges)}`, state: { n, edges } };
yield { line: 2, label: `init adj — ${n} empty buckets`, state: { adj: adj.map(a => [...a]) } };
yield { line: 6, label: `undirected edge ${u}<->${v} — push both directions`, state: { adj: adj.map(a => [...a]) } };
yield { line: 9, label: 'init seen=[false,...], count=0', state: { adj: adj.map(a => [...a]), seen: [...seen], count } };
yield { line: 14, label: `outer scan i=${i} — seen[${i}]=${seen[i]}`, state: { adj: adj.map(a => [...a]), seen: [...seen], count, i } };
yield { line: 15, label: `unvisited — count → ${count}, launch dfs(${i})`, state: { adj: adj.map(a => [...a]), seen: [...seen], count, i } };
yield { line: 11, label: `mark ${u} seen`, state: { adj: adj.map(a => [...a]), seen: [...seen], count, current: u, stackSize: stack.length } };
yield { line: 12, label: `neighbor ${v} unvisited — push to stack`, state: { adj: adj.map(a => [...a]), seen: [...seen], count, current: u, stackSize: stack.length } };
yield { line: 15, label: `component ${count} fully explored`, state: { adj: adj.map(a => [...a]), seen: [...seen], count } };
yield { line: 18, label: `return ${count}`, state: { seen: [...seen], count, returns: count } };

notes: Push BOTH directions when building adj — the graph is undirected.
Increment count exactly when you START a new DFS from an unvisited node.
Union-Find (DSU) is an alternative: O((V + E) * α(V)). DFS is simpler when you already have the adjacency list.

alternates.label: Union-Find (DSU)
alternates.when: Prefer Union-Find when edges arrive as a stream and you must report the component count after each addition — DFS would need to rebuild the adjacency list and re-scan from scratch. For a fully batched edge list like this problem, DFS and UF are equivalent; UF requires no adjacency list.
notes: No adjacency list needed — each edge is consumed directly as a union(u, v) call.
Decrement count only on a successful union (different roots); same-root edges are already in one component.
Path compression (halving) keeps amortized find near O(α(n)) — effectively constant for any practical n.

questions.q: Why push both adj[u].push(v) AND adj[v].push(u)?
options: Pushing both halves the DFS recursion depth by letting it descend either neighbor first
The graph is undirected — edges connect in both directions
It deduplicates parallel edges by ensuring each endpoint records the connection symmetrically
DFS needs each edge in both directions to compute correct in-degree and out-degree counts

questions.q: When do you increment the component count?
options: When you launch a new dfs from an unvisited node
Each time the recursion stack unwinds back to depth 0
